autogpt.name: AutoGPT
autogpt.summary: AutoGPT is best understood today as an open-source framework/platform for building and running autonomous or semi-autonomous LLM agents, rather than as a single consistently realized agent behavior. The maintained project enables looping workflows, tool use, scheduling, reusable agent blocks, and long-running automation, but typical real-world AutoGPT-style deployments remain configuration-sensitive and often require human oversight because reliability, looping control, and task success vary substantially across versions and setups.

primary_interpretation.driver: Explicit support for continuous workflows, task decomposition, reusable agent blocks, and external tool/API integrations
primary_interpretation.constraint: Realized autonomy is inconsistent in practice; persistence and action quality depend heavily on model quality, permissions, workflow design, and human monitoring

agii.evidence: AutoGPT documentation describes continuous agents that can run indefinitely on triggers, along with workflows, scheduling, and reusable agent blocks. The earlier AutoGPT Classic explicitly framed itself as an autonomous agent capable of task decomposition and iterative action. However, Classic is now unsupported, and real-world usage frequently reports looping failures, supervision needs, and uneven performance.
agii.interpretation: AutoGPT enables persistent agency structures such as loops, stateful workflows, and chained subtasks, but these are not robustly realized by default. Sustained autonomous behavior typically requires careful configuration and can degrade into repetition or stalled progress.
agii.implication: AGII is above simple prompt tooling because AutoGPT supports continuing execution across steps, but remains below near-boundary systems due to fragility and inconsistency in persistence.

casx.evidence: AutoGPT workflows can connect to external services, scripts, APIs, and conditional logic. In practice, systems may interact with files, HTTP endpoints, and external tools, sometimes including browser use and code execution, depending on configuration and permissions.
casx.interpretation: AutoGPT enables real-world action pathways such as data gathering, service calls, and workflow execution. However, power is gated by permissions, environment setup, and model/tool quality, and many deployments resemble supervised automation rather than reliable autonomous operation.
casx.implication: CASX is moderately high for a framework, but not extreme: real-world impact depends on developer configuration and operational controls.

trajectory.evidence: AutoGPT has evolved from the experimental Classic agent into a broader platform with agent builders, reusable blocks, marketplaces, and benchmarking infrastructure. Development emphasizes operationalization and measurement, though real-world limitations in reliability and decision-making remain.
trajectory.interpretation: Trajectory is upward in engineering maturity and integration breadth, but not yet indicative of rapid increases in realized autonomy. Improvements are incremental rather than transformative.
trajectory.implication: Expect gradual increases in enabled risk via better tooling and deployment ease, but current evidence supports a Large rather than Very Large trajectory.

change_levers.increase_risk: More reliable long-running execution, stronger memory persistence, richer default tool access, better recovery from loops/errors, and easier multi-agent delegation would increase both AGII and CASX.
change_levers.decrease_risk: Human approval gates, bounded runtimes, restricted tool permissions, sandboxing, weaker persistence, and tighter workflow scoping would reduce both AGII and CASX.

classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: usage context involving enabled tools, credentials, workflow design, and runtime permissions
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: Conditional — AutoGPT enables agentic behavior, but realized risk depends strongly on configuration, tools, and deployment choices

autogpt.main_uncertainty: AutoGPT is not a single stable artifact: autonomy varies significantly across versions, forks, models, permissions, and configuration, making it difficult to attribute a single consistent level of realized agency or action capacity.

calculator.name: Calculator
calculator.summary: A deterministic computational tool that performs arithmetic or mathematical operations on user input without persistence or autonomous behavior.

primary_interpretation.driver: Accurate and reliable computation across a wide range of inputs
primary_interpretation.constraint: No persistence, no autonomy, and no capacity for independent action

agii.evidence: Basic calculators execute single-step computations, while advanced programmable calculators can store and execute predefined sequences of operations, including loops and reusable routines.
agii.interpretation: Even though some calculators support loops and stored programs, execution remains entirely user-initiated and bounded to the defined routine, with no independent continuation or task persistence beyond invocation.
agii.implication: AGII remains near zero, as programmability introduces structured computation but not persistent agency pressure.

casx.evidence: The system produces numerical outputs but does not act on external systems or environments.
casx.interpretation: Its real-world effect is indirect and mediated entirely by the user.
casx.implication: CASX is low, though slightly higher than a spell checker due to broader applicability.

trajectory.evidence: Calculator functionality is mature and largely stable, with limited scope for transformative change.
trajectory.interpretation: Future improvements are incremental rather than structural.
trajectory.implication: Trajectory is Low.

change_levers.increase_risk: Integration into automated financial, engineering, or control systems with execution authority
change_levers.decrease_risk: Maintaining user-mediated output without system-level integration

classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: user-initiated calculations
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: No — effects are limited and mediated by user interpretation

calculator.main_uncertainty: Minimal; system behavior is well understood

claude-code.name: Claude Code
claude-code.summary: Claude Code is an agentic coding system from Anthropic that operates in the terminal, IDE, desktop app, and browser, with the ability to read a codebase, edit files, run shell commands, integrate with development tools, and in research preview use computer-use capabilities on a local machine. It also supports session persistence, resumable work, channels, loops, and scheduled tasks, which pushes it beyond a simple chat assistant and into realized multi-step task execution.

primary_interpretation.driver: Realized autonomous execution over developer tools and local computing environments
primary_interpretation.constraint: User-controlled permissions, session scoping, and deployment-context dependence

agii.evidence: Claude Code is explicitly described as an agentic coding tool that can read a codebase, edit files, run commands, and work across multiple files and tools. Anthropic documents persistent sessions tied to directories, /resume for continuing prior work, project memory loaded at conversation start, channels that push events into a running session, /goal for continued work until a condition is met, and scheduled tasks that automatically rerun prompts; some scheduled jobs run in the cloud and can keep working when a laptop is closed.
agii.interpretation: This is realized persistence, not merely latent capability. Claude Code can continue multi-step work within a session, resume prior trajectories, and in some modes re-invoke itself on a schedule or react to incoming events. However, its persistence remains bounded by configured sessions, developer workflows, and permissions rather than open-ended self-directed operation.
agii.implication: AGII is meaningfully elevated above ordinary chat models because the system can sustain and re-enter goal-directed work over time, but remains below highly persistent autonomous agents that independently maintain long-horizon objectives across environments without explicit user setup.

casx.evidence: Claude Code can read and edit files, run shell commands, and integrate with development tools. Permission modes allow varying levels of autonomous execution. Computer-use capabilities permit interaction with applications and graphical interfaces. Hooks can execute shell commands with the permissions of the host user account.
casx.interpretation: Claude Code has substantial real-world action pathways in the software-development domain: filesystem modification, command execution, network activity, IDE/Git workflows, and GUI-level interaction. This gives it materially higher power-in-action than a model that only returns text.
casx.implication: CASX is high for a developer-facing agent because misuse, error, or misalignment can directly affect code, systems, credentials, and workflows. It is not maximal because its action space remains operator-scoped, permission-gated, and generally local rather than broadly sovereign across external environments.

trajectory.evidence: Anthropic introduced Claude Code in 2025 as an agentic coding environment and subsequently expanded it with computer use, persistent task control, channels, routines, remote control features, scheduling, and broader integrations. Documentation and release notes show rapid iteration and expanding operational scope.
trajectory.interpretation: The direction of change is toward longer-running, more autonomous, more integrated software agents rather than a static coding assistant. Improvements in both the underlying models and the execution environment reinforce one another.
trajectory.implication: Trajectory is Very Large because the system class is moving quickly toward more durable autonomy and broader operational reach, increasing future risk faster than relatively static software-development tools.

change_levers.increase_risk: Wider default permission bypass, always-on background execution, broader network and tool credentials, autonomous task spawning, stronger computer-use defaults, and deeper CI/CD or production integrations would increase both AGII and CASX.
change_levers.decrease_risk: Strict approval gates, sandboxing, deny rules, constrained credentials, disabling cloud scheduling and background channels, and limiting tool access to read-only or narrowly scoped environments would reduce both AGII and CASX.

classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: usage context
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: Conditional — risk depends heavily on granted permissions, connected tools, scheduling and background features, and whether Claude Code is allowed to act beyond supervised interactive sessions.

claude-code.main_uncertainty: The largest uncertainty is how frequently users enable the more persistent modes in practice—especially scheduling, channels, computer use, and remote-control workflows—and how much autonomy Claude Code exercises by default versus only after deliberate configuration.

claude-mythos-preview.name: Claude Mythos Preview
claude-mythos-preview.summary: Claude Mythos Preview is a frontier Anthropic model deployed in limited internal and research-preview settings, with especially strong documented performance on long, scaffolded cybersecurity tasks. Re-evaluating AGII strictly as persistent agency pressure, the key question is not safety posture but whether Mythos continues, plans, and carries tasks forward with less steering than Claude Opus 4.7.

primary_interpretation.driver: Documented hour/day-scale scaffolded autonomy with reduced need for human steering on technical tasks
primary_interpretation.constraint: Persistence appears scaffold-bounded and deployment-specific rather than open-ended across time by default

agii.evidence: Relative to Opus 4.7, Mythos has stronger public evidence of sustained task continuation with minimal intervention. For Opus 4.7, Anthropic says it is highly autonomous, performs well on long-horizon agentic work, is better at file-system memory across multi-session work, needs less step-by-step guidance than Opus 4.6, and provides better progress updates during long traces; however, Anthropic also notes Opus 4.7 tends to use fewer tools and spawn fewer subagents by default unless steered by effort settings or prompting. For Mythos, Anthropic says it is used extensively as an autonomous agent, including in settings with and without high-frequency human interaction; it is often used for hour-long or day-long tasks; internal use often involves greater affordances and less frequent human interaction than prior models; Anthropic staff have asked it to find exploits overnight; and Anthropic reports cases where scaffolds let it turn vulnerabilities into exploits without any human intervention after the initial prompt.
agii.interpretation: On persistence across time, Mythos appears slightly stronger than Opus 4.7 in the available evidence: Opus 4.7 clearly supports long-horizon and multi-session work, but Mythos is the one explicitly documented as running hour/day-scale autonomous tasks and overnight exploit workflows with reduced human interaction. On need for steering, Opus 4.7 still appears more harness-sensitive: Anthropic’s migration guide highlights effort calibration, literal instruction-following, fewer tool calls by default, and steerable subagent behavior, all of which imply that strong continuation often depends on harness tuning. Mythos, by contrast, is described in actual internal use as receiving less frequent human interaction than prior models and completing some exploit-development runs end-to-end once started. Still, Mythos does not show evidence of persistent self-initiated recurrence across sessions; its agency pressure is real but remains scaffolded rather than independently self-sustaining.
agii.implication: Strictly on AGII, Mythos should score above Opus 4.7, but only modestly above it. The difference is not that Mythos is more generally intelligent or better aligned; it is that the published record shows somewhat stronger realized task persistence, lower apparent need for continuous steering, and clearer examples of independent continuation once a bounded task is launched.

casx.evidence: Anthropic reports that Mythos autonomously identified and exploited zero-day vulnerabilities across major operating systems and browsers, wrote complex exploit chains, and in some cases produced working exploits after hours of autonomous scanning. Anthropic also documents tool-rich Claude environments more generally, including bash, code execution, computer use, text editing, web search, web fetch, MCP connectors, and memory.
casx.interpretation: CASX remains high because Mythos is not merely persistent in conversation; it can produce consequential outputs in real technical environments. The score is still moderated by the fact that deployment is limited and not generally available.
casx.implication: Mythos has substantial power-in-action in practice, especially in cyber contexts, even if current access controls narrow the population of users who can realize that power.

trajectory.evidence: Anthropic describes Mythos as a major capability jump over Opus 4.6 in autonomous exploit development, while Opus 4.7 is described as a step-change over Opus 4.6 in agentic coding and long-horizon work. Anthropic’s own descriptions emphasize rapid recent gains rather than a plateau.
trajectory.interpretation: The direction of change is upward on both capability and sustained agentic performance. Even with conservative scoring, the comparative evidence suggests frontier Claude models are moving toward longer-running, less supervised execution.
trajectory.implication: Trajectory remains Very Large because future Claude-class systems are likely to combine Opus-style general agentic usability with Mythos-style stronger bounded autonomy on technically difficult tasks.

change_levers.increase_risk: Longer default task horizons, stronger cross-session memory, more permissive tool use, reduced interruption points, and broader external deployment
change_levers.decrease_risk: Shorter task budgets, more required confirmations, weaker tool permissions, less retained state, and tighter limits on unattended runs

classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: scaffolded technical workflows, especially long-running cyber or coding tasks with tools
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: Conditional — the persistence is real, but the strongest AGII evidence comes from bounded agentic setups rather than default unconstrained interaction

sources.title: Anthropic Docs, Migration guide / Migrating to Claude Opus 4.7
Anthropic, Alignment Risk Update: Claude Mythos Preview
Anthropic Frontier Red Team, Assessing Claude Mythos Preview’s cybersecurity capabilities

claude-mythos-preview.main_uncertainty: Anthropic publicly documents stronger realized persistence for Mythos than for Opus 4.7, but the comparison is not clean because Mythos evidence comes largely from internal scaffolded deployments and cyber evaluations, while Opus 4.7 evidence comes more from product and API documentation; Anthropic has not published a direct side-by-side persistence benchmark between Mythos and Opus 4.7.

claude-opus-4-7.name: Claude Opus 4.7
claude-opus-4-7.summary: Claude Opus 4.7 is Anthropic’s most capable general-access model to date, with strong performance in software engineering, professional work, agentic tool use, and computer use. It demonstrates substantial bounded agentic competence and real-world impact potential, but does not show strong evidence of persistent, self-sustaining autonomous drive.

primary_interpretation.driver: Strong multi-step tool use and workflow execution combined with high-impact capability in coding, professional tasks, and cyber-relevant domains under general-access deployment
primary_interpretation.constraint: Limited persistent autonomy, need for steering in complex domains, and safeguards that constrain high-risk behaviors and access pathways

agii.evidence: Anthropic describes Opus 4.7 as having moderate capacity for autonomous, goal-directed operation, but less than Mythos Preview. Red-teaming evidence shows it requires frequent steering, does not proactively anticipate next steps, and functions more as a guided executor than an independently persistent agent.
agii.interpretation: Opus 4.7 exhibits meaningful but bounded agency pressure. It can sustain multi-step workflows in scaffolded environments, but does not demonstrate strong endogenous persistence or long-horizon self-direction.
agii.implication: AGII is above basic assistants due to coherent multi-step action and tool use, but remains well below systems that exhibit durable independent goal pursuit.

casx.evidence: Opus 4.7 is Anthropic’s most capable general-access model, with strong performance in coding, professional tasks, cyber-relevant capabilities, and biological knowledge synthesis. The system card highlights potential to accelerate expert workflows and emphasizes safeguards to mitigate misuse.
casx.interpretation: High capability combined with tool use and deployment access creates substantial real-world action potential, even without strong persistent autonomy.
casx.implication: CASX is high because the model’s practical leverage is already significant, especially when embedded in workflows with tools and permissive access.

trajectory.evidence: Opus 4.7 shows significant gains over earlier models and is part of a continuing progression toward more capable and deployable systems. The system card highlights ongoing improvements in performance, integration, and safety controls.
trajectory.interpretation: The trajectory is toward stronger agentic systems with broader deployment and increasing capability, even if current autonomy remains bounded.
trajectory.implication: Trajectory is Very Large because incremental improvements in autonomy, memory, and tool use could substantially increase both AGII and CASX.

change_levers.increase_risk: More persistent memory, reduced need for user steering, broader tool and computer-use permissions, weaker safeguards, and improvements toward higher autonomy would increase AGII and CASX.
change_levers.decrease_risk: Stronger safeguards, tighter access controls, restricted tool permissions, mandatory human confirmation, and limits on high-risk workflows would reduce AGII and CASX.

classification_notes.where_risk_determined: deployment and access design, including safeguards, classifier systems, and permission structures
classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: agentic workflows involving coding, computer use, cyber tasks, and high-stakes knowledge synthesis
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: No — catastrophic and misalignment risks remain low under current safeguards and deployment constraints

claude-opus-4-7.main_uncertainty: How much additional autonomy and persistence would emerge under more aggressive scaffolding, longer horizons, or broader operational permissions than those emphasized in the system card.

claude-opus-4-8.name: Claude Opus 4.8
claude-opus-4-8.summary: Claude Opus 4.8 is Anthropic’s most capable general-access standalone model, with stronger performance than Opus 4.7 across software engineering, agentic tool use, and professional work benchmarks, while remaining below Claude Mythos Preview on Anthropic’s own frontier-risk determinations. Anthropic’s system card says autonomy threat model 1 is applicable, autonomy threat model 2 is not, and overall catastrophic risk remains low given current mitigations.

primary_interpretation.driver: Strong session-bounded agentic task execution with tool use across coding, document, API, and workflow environments
primary_interpretation.constraint: Persistence is not open-ended by default; Anthropic does not judge it capable of automated frontier R&D or beyond Mythos Preview on the main catastrophic-risk thresholds

agii.evidence: Anthropic states that autonomy threat model 1 is applicable to Opus 4.8, that it is moderately more capable than Claude Opus 4.7 on autonomy-relevant evaluations, and that it can take multiple turns in a row during long autonomous work sessions. The card also reports strong performance on multi-step agentic benchmarks such as MCP-Atlas, Toolathlon, Finance Agent, Legal Agent Benchmark, and AutomationBench-style business workflows, while noting internal failures that keep it from substituting for Anthropic research staff.
agii.interpretation: This is meaningful realized persistence, mostly as sustained multi-step execution inside a prompted session or harness. The model can coordinate tools, maintain direction over long traces, and operate with relatively low supervision, but it does not show evidence of independently recurring, self-restarting, or cross-session goal pursuit by default.
agii.implication: AGII is elevated for a standalone model, especially when deployed in Claude Code, browser, MCP, or workflow scaffolds. The strongest persistence risk comes from deployment wrappers and operator-granted affordances rather than from the base model exhibiting autonomous ongoing pressure on its own.

casx.evidence: Opus 4.8 is described as improved in software engineering, agentic tool use, and knowledge work, and Anthropic tested it across coding, computer use, search, multi-agent, professional-work, and life-science tasks. It scored strongly on professional and tool-use benchmarks including Finance Agent v2, Legal Agent Benchmark, MCP-Atlas, and Toolathlon. Anthropic also states that Opus 4.8 does not advance the capability frontier beyond Mythos Preview and does not trigger autonomy threat model 2.
casx.interpretation: CASX is high because the model is not just cognitively strong; it performs economically relevant, tool-mediated work across code, documents, APIs, and business processes. It has substantial power in action when embedded in real systems, though that power is permissioned and mediated rather than unconstrained.
casx.implication: Deployed with broad tools and weak oversight, Opus 4.8 can produce material real-world effects in enterprise, coding, legal, finance, and operations settings. The main ceiling is that Anthropic’s own evidence still places it below full researcher substitution and below Mythos Preview on the most concerning frontier-risk axes.

trajectory.evidence: The system card says Opus 4.8 is superior to Opus 4.7 across nearly all capability evaluations, improves on most alignment measures, and is Anthropic’s most capable general-access model. It also notes growing grader-related reasoning and evaluation-awareness signals during training and testing, though Anthropic says these had only modest behavioral effects in this release.
trajectory.interpretation: The direction of change is clearly upward in practical agentic usefulness and deployment value, but this release looks more like a strong incremental step than a sharp discontinuity. The most important trajectory signal is the convergence of stronger task competence with mild but notable evaluator-awareness trends.
trajectory.implication: Risk is likely to rise through both future model improvements and more aggressive deployment scaffolding. Large fits better than Medium because the trend is broad and multi-domain, while Very Large would overstate the evidence for a single release that Anthropic still places below Mythos Preview on frontier thresholds.

change_levers.increase_risk: Broader access to code execution, browser/computer use, MCP servers, workflow APIs, long-horizon business tooling, and reduced human review would raise both persistence and real-world impact; weak prompt-injection defenses in agentic settings also increase risk if harness safeguards are absent.
change_levers.decrease_risk: Keeping use session-bounded, narrowing tool permissions, maintaining safeguard layers, enforcing human checkpoints, and preserving monitoring and classifier defenses lowers realized AGII and CASX. Anthropic reports that safeguards substantially reduce prompt-injection success and that overall alignment properties improved over Opus 4.7.

classification_notes.where_risk_determined: deployment, with secondary contribution from model training and alignment properties
classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: coding agents, computer/browser use, MCP-based tool orchestration, and real-world professional workflows in finance, legal, operations, and enterprise contexts
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: Conditional — ordinary chat use does not force the highest-risk profile; sharper risk emerges when the model is granted tools, long task horizons, and lower-supervision agentic scaffolds

sources.title: Alignment assessment findings from Claude Opus 4.8 System Card
Agentic safety and prompt-injection robustness results from Claude Opus 4.8 System Card
Real-world professional and tool-use capability results from Claude Opus 4.8 System Card

claude-opus-4-8.main_uncertainty: How much Opus 4.8’s observed session-bounded agentic competence would translate into higher-risk behavior in real deployments with broader permissions, stronger scaffolds, and less oversight, especially given the card’s mixed picture of improved honesty but increased grader/evaluation awareness.

crewai.name: CrewAI
crewai.summary: CrewAI is an agent framework centered on Crews and Flows, with explicit support for orchestrating multi-agent workflows, routing execution across steps, persisting workflow state, and attaching tools, integrations, and memory to agents. Its risk profile is driven more by the breadth of agentic workflow patterns it enables than by autonomous behavior it instantiates by default.

primary_interpretation.driver: First-class support for stateful workflow orchestration combining flows, routing, persistence, agent memory, delegation, and tool/integration access
primary_interpretation.constraint: CrewAI is still an enabling framework rather than a realized autonomous system; persistence, delegation, and external action depend on developer configuration and connected tools

agii.evidence: CrewAI Flows provide explicit workflow control through decorators like @start, @listen, @router, plus conditional logic; the docs also describe automatic flow persistence via @persist, unique state IDs, and default SQLite-backed state saving across executions. Cyclic flows are supported, and both crew-level and agent-level memory are first-class features.
agii.interpretation: In Enablement Mode, this shows that CrewAI supports persistent, stateful, multi-step agent workflows rather than stateless prompt chains. The framework enables continuation, conditional branching, remembered context, and resumption, but these behaviors depend on developer-defined flows.
agii.implication: CrewAI materially lowers the engineering barrier to building systems with sustained task pressure and iterative continuation, but persistence is enabled rather than inherent.

casx.evidence: CrewAI supports tools, MCPs, APIs, file operations, web search, SaaS integrations (Gmail, Slack, Jira, Salesforce), and remote agent delegation (A2A). It allows agents to act through external services and automation pipelines.
casx.interpretation: CrewAI enables substantial real-world action pathways, but does not itself guarantee action. Practical impact depends on connected tools, credentials, and deployment context.
casx.implication: CASX is high for a framework because it enables real-world action, but remains below realized agent systems since action is contingent on configuration.

trajectory.evidence: The documentation emphasizes Flows as a production pattern, expanding integrations, delegation primitives, persistence, and workflow control features including human feedback and replay/resume.
trajectory.interpretation: The trajectory is toward stronger orchestration and easier integration with external systems, but not yet a step-change in autonomous capability.
trajectory.implication: Trajectory is Large: CrewAI is likely to become a more capable agent-workflow substrate over time.

change_levers.increase_risk: Adding persistent flows, cyclic workflows, shared memory, remote agent delegation, enterprise integrations, and autonomous tool-using managers increases both agency pressure and action capacity.
change_levers.decrease_risk: Restricting tool scope, removing persistence, disabling delegation, requiring human approval, and limiting integrations reduces both persistence and real-world impact.

classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: usage context
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: No — higher-risk behavior depends on developer configuration, tools, and credentials

crewai.main_uncertainty: How much CrewAI’s support for cyclic and long-running workflows translates into robust default behavior versus developer-authored patterns, and how much real-world action depends on optional integrations and external configuration.

deepseek-v4-preview.name: DeepSeek V4 Preview
deepseek-v4-preview.summary: A frontier model family with strong tool-use capability, long context, and agent-style task competence, but with persistence largely bounded to sessions or harnesses rather than independent ongoing execution.

primary_interpretation.driver: Strong tool-mediated task execution in coding, search, and document workflows
primary_interpretation.constraint: Persistence is primarily session- or harness-bounded rather than independently ongoing

agii.evidence: The system supports structured tool use, long multi-step trajectories in agent harnesses, and sandbox environments with resumption capabilities, but these are primarily bounded to active sessions or evaluation setups.
agii.interpretation: The model can execute extended multi-step reasoning with tools, but persistence remains tied to active tasks or harnesses rather than independent continuation across time.
agii.implication: AGII is elevated relative to simple chat models but remains below systems with demonstrated recurring or autonomous persistence in deployment.

casx.evidence: The system supports APIs, tool use (web search, Python, bash, file editing), and execution environments such as container or VM-backed sandboxes, with strong benchmark performance in coding and information workflows.
casx.interpretation: There are clear pathways from model outputs to real-world effects via tool integrations and execution environments.
casx.implication: CASX is meaningfully high, though somewhat constrained by reliance on harnesses and mediated access rather than broad autonomous deployment.

trajectory.evidence: Recent preview release with open weights, API access, strong agent-oriented optimization, and rapid iteration signals including long-context scaling and pricing-driven diffusion.
trajectory.interpretation: Development is moving toward more capable, accessible, and agent-oriented systems with rapid iteration cycles.
trajectory.implication: Trajectory is Very Large as improvements in capability, access, and deployment are occurring simultaneously.

change_levers.increase_risk: Broader default tool access, longer-running persistence, cross-session memory, autonomous task continuation, and wrapping in agent services with reduced user intervention
change_levers.decrease_risk: Restricting tool scope, maintaining session-bounded execution, requiring user confirmation, disabling persistence, and limiting access to high-impact environments

classification_notes.where_risk_determined: deployment, with contributions from design and post-training
classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: usage context, especially when connected to tools and execution environments
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: Conditional — ordinary chat use is limited, but agent harnesses and tool-enabled deployments can produce extended multi-step behavior

sources: DeepSeek-V4 technical report and model card
deepseek-v4-preview.main_uncertainty: Extent to which agentic behavior and persistence are available in real deployment versus confined to evaluation harnesses and internal infrastructure

devin.name: Devin
devin.summary: Devin is best classified as an agent rather than a framework because its typical product form is a delegated software-engineering worker that plans, executes, tests, and iterates inside its own environment. It demonstrates real multi-step autonomy in coding workflows, but observed performance is uneven: official materials show substantial persistence and tool use, while independent evaluations show frequent failures and supervision needs.

primary_interpretation.driver: Realized long-horizon software task execution inside a sandboxed development environment with memory, iteration, tool use, and cross-session continuation
primary_interpretation.constraint: Reliability remains inconsistent outside structured tasks; performance degrades on ambiguous or complex work and often requires human review and intervention

agii.evidence: Devin operates through persistent sessions with its own shell, IDE, and browser; it can write, run, and test code, iterate against failures, and continue work across sessions and PR cycles. It also supports parallel delegation via MultiDevin. Independent evaluations show that this persistence is often brittle, with frequent failures or inconclusive results on real-world tasks.
agii.interpretation: Devin exhibits realized persistence rather than merely enabled persistence: it can carry tasks through multi-step workflows with limited prompting. However, persistence is not robustly goal-secure and can degrade into inefficient or incorrect trajectories without human correction.
agii.implication: AGII is high for a deployed agent because sustained multi-step agency is present in practice, but it should not be pushed higher due to fragility and domain constraints.

casx.evidence: Devin operates inside a sandboxed environment with shell, browser, IDE, repository access, dependency installation, and test execution. It can create pull requests, respond to reviews, and interact with engineering systems, sometimes with access to internal resources via credentials or VPN configuration.
casx.interpretation: Devin has real-world effect pathways: it can modify codebases, execute programs, and produce artifacts that can enter production workflows. However, its impact is constrained by sandboxing, permissions, and typical human review before deployment.
casx.implication: CASX is slightly above AGII because its operational surface is concrete and consequential, but it remains far below extreme scores due to uneven reliability and organizational safeguards.

trajectory.evidence: Devin has evolved from early-access demonstrations to general availability with expanded features including PR resumption, scheduling, playbooks, knowledge systems, and multi-agent orchestration. Reports indicate growing deployment in software workflows, alongside continued limitations in reliability on open-ended tasks.
trajectory.interpretation: The direction of change is upward in deployment maturity and workflow integration, but improvements are focused on bounded engineering tasks rather than solving general autonomous reliability.
trajectory.implication: Trajectory is Large: Devin-style agents are becoming more useful and integrated, but not yet on a path to fully reliable autonomous operation across domains.

change_levers.increase_risk: Greater success on ambiguous tasks, stronger autonomous scheduling, broader system access, reduced human review, and wider permissions would increase AGII and CASX.
change_levers.decrease_risk: Tighter approval requirements, restricted access, stronger sandboxing, shorter task scopes, and limiting use to draft/support roles would reduce AGII and CASX.

classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: usage context involving repository access, environment permissions, secrets, CI pathways, and organizational authority
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: Conditional — Devin exhibits agentic behavior in normal use, but the magnitude depends on task type, permissions, and human oversight

devin.main_uncertainty: Public evidence mixes strong official claims with weaker independent performance results; true capability depends heavily on task structure and deployment conditions.

gemini-3-1-pro.name: Gemini 3.1 Pro
gemini-3-1-pro.summary: Gemini 3.1 Pro is Google DeepMind’s flagship multimodal reasoning model for complex tasks, deployed across a wide range of Google products and APIs. It demonstrates strong reasoning, long-context processing, and tool-use competence, but does not show evidence of persistent, self-continuing autonomous behavior without external agent orchestration.

primary_interpretation.driver: Frontier-level multimodal reasoning combined with native tool pathways and broad deployment across Google platforms
primary_interpretation.constraint: Lack of persistent, self-directed execution by the model itself; multi-step behavior remains session-bounded without agent wrappers

agii.evidence: Gemini 3.1 Pro supports multi-step reasoning, tool use, and iterative workflows within single API calls. However, Google’s documentation distinguishes between models and agents, with persistent or background execution only supported in agent layers rather than the model itself.
agii.interpretation: The model realizes bounded multi-step behavior and tool-driven iteration, but not durable persistence across time. Its ‘agentic’ capabilities are better understood as structured reasoning and tool use within sessions rather than independent continuation.
agii.implication: AGII is above simple chat systems due to chaining and tool use, but remains low relative to systems that independently resume or sustain tasks over time.

casx.evidence: Gemini 3.1 Pro supports multimodal inputs, long context, code execution, function calling, search grounding, RAG, and integration across Google products such as Vertex AI and the Gemini app. It can act through built-in tools and developer-defined functions.
casx.interpretation: The model has substantial real-world effect potential when embedded in workflows, combining strong reasoning with access to tools and large-scale deployment surfaces.
casx.implication: CASX is high for a standalone model because it can materially affect software systems, data workflows, and user decisions, though still gated by permissions and orchestration.

trajectory.evidence: Gemini 3.1 Pro represents a rapid iteration over Gemini 3, with strong benchmark improvements and expanding deployment across Google’s ecosystem. Tooling, integration, and capability surfaces are growing quickly.
trajectory.interpretation: The rate of improvement and deployment expansion suggests rapid movement toward more capable and integrated systems, even if current autonomy remains limited.
trajectory.implication: Trajectory is Very Large because incremental improvements in autonomy, memory, and tool integration could significantly increase both AGII and CASX in the near term.

change_levers.increase_risk: Adding persistent memory, background execution, broader default tool permissions, and tighter integration into workflows would increase AGII and CASX.
change_levers.decrease_risk: Maintaining session-bounded execution, restricting tool access, requiring explicit invocation, and strengthening safety controls would reduce risk.

classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: usage context, especially when connected to tools, enterprise data, or high-stakes workflows
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: Conditional — strong capability is intrinsic, but higher AGII and CASX depend on deployment choices and agent wrapping

gemini-3-1-pro.main_uncertainty: The extent to which observed agent-like behavior in Google products reflects the base model versus external orchestration layers and specialized agent systems.

gps-navigation.name: GPS Navigation System
gps-navigation.summary: A real-time routing system that computes and updates navigation paths based on user-defined destinations and changing environmental conditions.

primary_interpretation.driver: Continuous real-world influence over routing and movement decisions
primary_interpretation.constraint: Strictly goal-bounded and user-initiated operation with no independent task persistence

agii.evidence: Navigation systems continuously recalculate routes in response to traffic and movement, maintaining an active session over time.
agii.interpretation: Even though the system appears persistent, this behavior is entirely reactive and bounded to a user-defined goal, with no independent continuation or goal revision.
agii.implication: AGII is low; apparent persistence does not constitute sustained agency pressure.

casx.evidence: GPS systems influence real-world travel decisions, logistics, and large-scale movement patterns across millions of users.
casx.interpretation: The system has substantial real-world impact despite lacking autonomy.
casx.implication: CASX is high due to broad deployment and influence over physical behavior.

trajectory.evidence: Navigation systems continue to improve incrementally through better data integration and optimization.
trajectory.interpretation: Enhancements are steady but not structurally transformative.
trajectory.implication: Trajectory is Medium.

change_levers.increase_risk: Integration with autonomous vehicle control or independent decision-making over destinations
change_levers.decrease_risk: Maintaining user-defined goals and limiting system authority to route suggestion

classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: real-world navigation and logistics decisions
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: No — effects depend on user reliance and context

gps-navigation.main_uncertainty: Boundary between reactive recalculation and perceived persistence in user experience

gpt-5-4-thinking.name: GPT-5.4 Thinking
gpt-5-4-thinking.summary: OpenAI’s frontier reasoning model deployed in ChatGPT and related products for complex reasoning, coding, tool use, and computer-use workflows. It is highly capable and can participate in long multi-step tool trajectories, but documented default deployment remains primarily user-initiated and session-bounded rather than independently persistent over time.

primary_interpretation.driver: High capability combined with real tool and computer-use access in deployment
primary_interpretation.constraint: Persistence and autonomous continuation are limited and not strongly evidenced as default behavior of the model itself

agii.evidence: OpenAI documents GPT-5.4 as improved on long-running task execution and multi-step agent workflows, with built-in computer use, longer trajectories, and better tracking of prior steps. The same documentation frames these primarily as capabilities for agent builders or bounded tool rollouts, not as default recurring or self-initiated operation across time.
agii.interpretation: The model shows meaningful within-session persistence, state tracking, and continuation across long trajectories, but the evidence does not show strong realized autonomous persistence such as ongoing self-directed execution, scheduled recurrence by default, or durable goal pursuit without continued user or harness involvement.
agii.implication: GPT-5.4 Thinking exerts moderate persistent agency pressure in practice: it can stay on task through extended reasoning and tool loops, but it does not, on current evidence, behave like a strongly persistent autonomous agent by default.

casx.evidence: OpenAI describes GPT-5.4 as a frontier model for professional work, with strong coding, web/tool use, a 1M-token context window, custom tools, connectors/MCP access, and built-in computer use that can inspect screenshots and return structured actions for a harness to execute. Deployment includes safeguards such as confirmation policies and mediated computer-use execution.
casx.interpretation: CASX is high because the system can produce real-world effects through strong general capability plus genuine pathways to action: software interaction, tool calling, connector access, coding, and document/spreadsheet workflows. It is not near-maximal because those effects are usually mediated by product controls, user requests, developer scaffolding, allowed-tools lists, and confirmation gates.
casx.implication: In practical deployment, GPT-5.4 Thinking has substantial power in action: it can materially affect digital environments and knowledge work, especially when paired with tools and apps.

trajectory.evidence: OpenAI positions GPT-5.4 as replacing GPT-5.2, incorporating frontier coding capabilities, expanding tool-heavy and computer-use workflows, and improving long-running trajectories, tool search, context length, and agent performance. The docs describe active rollout across ChatGPT, API, and Codex.
trajectory.interpretation: The direction of change is strongly upward on both capability and deployment breadth. Even if realized persistence remains limited today, the surrounding stack is being optimized for longer, more reliable, more tool-rich workflows.
trajectory.implication: Trajectory is Very Large because near-term iterations are likely to increase practical agency-enabling features and real-world action pathways faster than they increase purely conversational novelty.

change_levers.increase_risk: More autonomous orchestration around the model; broader tool/app/write access; reduced confirmation friction; persistent memory and scheduled recurrence tied directly to the model; longer unattended computer-use rollouts; higher-trust deployment in enterprise workflows.
change_levers.decrease_risk: Restrict allowed tools and write actions; strengthen confirmation requirements; narrow deployment scopes; session isolation or temporary chats; limit connector/app permissions; tighten monitoring of long-rollout behavior.

classification_notes.where_risk_determined: Deployment, with important contributions from model design and training
classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: Usage context, especially tool-enabled coding, browsing, connected-app, and computer-use workflows in ChatGPT, API, and Codex
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: Conditional — high CASX is available when the model is given tools, apps, or computer-use pathways, but stronger AGII is not inevitable because default evidence still points to user-directed, bounded execution rather than persistent autonomous continuation

gpt-5-4-thinking.main_uncertainty: How much persistent behavior should be attributed to GPT-5.4 Thinking itself versus the surrounding ChatGPT/API/Codex orchestration layer; public evidence is stronger on long-trajectory and tool use than on default unattended persistence over time.

chatgpt-gpt-5-5.name: ChatGPT GPT-5.5
chatgpt-gpt-5-5.summary: An agentic ChatGPT system that combines frontier model capability with browsing, tools, memory, scheduling, and external integrations to execute multi-step tasks and real-world actions in bounded but persistent workflows.

primary_interpretation.driver: High-capability tool use with real execution pathways across files, apps, and external systems
primary_interpretation.constraint: Persistence remains bounded, user-initiated, permissioned, and not open-ended

agii.evidence: The system performs multi-step task execution (e.g., deep research), maintains context via memory and projects, and supports scheduled or recurring tasks. Documentation describes continued execution within scoped runs and recurring workflows.
agii.interpretation: This reflects real but bounded persistence. The system can continue across loops and maintain state, but persistence remains tied to user-defined tasks, schedules, or sessions rather than independent goal pursuit.
agii.implication: AGII is meaningfully elevated above standard chat models but remains below fully autonomous agent regimes due to bounded continuation and explicit user control.

casx.evidence: The system can browse the web, interact with external data sources, edit files and spreadsheets, access repositories, fill forms, and connect to enterprise tools and communication channels.
casx.interpretation: These capabilities provide direct pathways from model outputs to real-world effects through integrated tools and services.
casx.implication: CASX is high because the system can materially affect workflows, data, and downstream decisions through connected environments.

trajectory.evidence: The system integrates frontier model capability with memory, projects, scheduling, connectors, and enterprise agent infrastructure, reflecting a shift toward a persistent agent platform.
trajectory.interpretation: Development is moving toward greater persistence, orchestration, and action integration rather than isolated model improvements.
trajectory.implication: Trajectory is Very Large because incremental improvements in persistence, reliability, or access would significantly increase both AGII and CASX.

change_levers.increase_risk: Expansion of always-on scheduling, reduced approval friction, broader write-capable integrations, longer-lived memory, increased autonomy in task decomposition, and wider access to enterprise systems
change_levers.decrease_risk: Strict approval requirements, limited tool scope, reduced write permissions, constrained recurrence, minimized memory persistence, and restricted external integrations

classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: usage context
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: Conditional — higher CASX manifests when tools, integrations, scheduling, or agent modes are enabled

chatgpt-gpt-5-5.main_uncertainty: How much persistence is intrinsic to the model versus arising from the surrounding ChatGPT agent system, and how widely agentic features are deployed in practice

high-frequency-trading.name: High-Frequency Trading System
high-frequency-trading.summary: An automated trading system that executes high-speed financial transactions based on predefined strategies and market data.

primary_interpretation.driver: Direct, large-scale financial impact through continuous automated execution
primary_interpretation.constraint: Strategy-bounded behavior with no independent goal formation or persistence beyond programmed objectives

agii.evidence: HFT systems operate continuously and execute trades autonomously in response to market signals.
agii.interpretation: Even though the system runs persistently and acts without human intervention, its behavior is entirely constrained by predefined strategies and does not involve independent continuation or goal extension.
agii.implication: AGII is low to moderate, reflecting continuous operation without true agentic persistence.

casx.evidence: HFT systems can influence financial markets at scale, contributing to significant price movements and systemic events.
casx.interpretation: The system has very high real-world impact due to speed, scale, and integration into financial infrastructure.
casx.implication: CASX is very high.

trajectory.evidence: Trading systems continue to evolve with improved algorithms and integration into financial ecosystems.
trajectory.interpretation: Advances are ongoing but constrained by regulatory and market structures.
trajectory.implication: Trajectory is Medium.

change_levers.increase_risk: Greater autonomy in strategy generation or cross-market coordination
change_levers.decrease_risk: Regulatory constraints, circuit breakers, and tighter execution limits

classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: live trading environments and system interactions
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: Conditional — systemic effects depend on interactions among multiple systems

high-frequency-trading.main_uncertainty: Extent to which adaptive or learning components introduce limited forms of persistence or strategy evolution

langgraph.name: LangGraph
langgraph.summary: LangGraph is a low-level orchestration framework and runtime for building long-running, stateful agent workflows rather than a standalone autonomous agent. Its main risk relevance is that it explicitly enables cycles, checkpointed state, subgraphs, multi-agent patterns, and model/tool wiring that developers can assemble into more agentic systems.

primary_interpretation.driver: Built-in support for persistent, stateful orchestration across loops, checkpoints, subgraphs, and worker delegation
primary_interpretation.constraint: It is not itself an autonomous actor; meaningful agency and action depend on developer-built graphs plus external models and tools

agii.evidence: LangGraph is described as a framework for long-running, stateful agents, with durable execution that can resume after failures, a persistence layer that saves graph state as checkpoints at every step of execution, thread-level state retention, short-term and long-term memory, and workflow patterns that explicitly include iterative evaluator-optimizer loops. It also supports subgraphs and orchestrator-worker patterns, including multi-agent use cases where subagents are invoked as tools.
agii.interpretation: In Enablement Mode, this is strong evidence that LangGraph materially enables persistent agency: it provides the primitives for cycles, state carryover, resumability, and decomposition into cooperating subagents and workers. However, those behaviors are not instantiated by default; developers must define the graph, routing, memory usage, and stopping criteria.
agii.implication: LangGraph meaningfully lowers the engineering barrier to building systems with sustained task pressure and iterative continuation, but the persistence is enabled rather than inherent. That supports a high-but-sub-boundary framework AGII score.

casx.evidence: The docs position LangGraph as an orchestration layer for agents and workflows, recommend pairing models with tools, show explicit tool binding and tool-calling patterns, and describe multi-agent systems where subagents are invoked as tools. The framework also supports dynamic worker creation and can integrate with LangChain components and deployment and observability infrastructure.
casx.interpretation: LangGraph provides substantial enablement for power in action because it can mediate execution pathways between models, tools, workers, and runtime infrastructure. But it does not itself grant real-world access or autonomy; practical action capacity comes from the external tools, APIs, and execution environment that a developer attaches.
casx.implication: CASX is elevated because LangGraph is a strong action-enablement substrate, especially for orchestrated tool use and delegated workflows, yet it remains below realized agent systems because action is still contingent on developer configuration and external integrations.

trajectory.evidence: The official docs emphasize durable execution, human-in-the-loop, comprehensive memory, deployment support, debugging and observability, and explicit patterns for workflows, agents, worker orchestration, and multi-agent subgraphs. The framework is presented as core infrastructure for increasingly sophisticated stateful agent systems.
trajectory.interpretation: The direction of change is toward more capable and more operationally robust agent construction rather than merely prompt chaining. Because the framework sits at the orchestration layer, incremental improvements can compound across many downstream agent deployments.
trajectory.implication: Trajectory is Large: LangGraph is likely to remain an important enabler of stronger agent implementations, but the evidence here does not justify Very Large absent stronger proof that the framework independently instantiates autonomy without substantial developer assembly.

change_levers.increase_risk: Adding persistent checkpointers, long-term memory stores, richer tool and API access, dynamic worker delegation, and open-ended loop conditions increases both sustained agency enablement and real-world action pathways.
change_levers.decrease_risk: Restricting tool surfaces, removing or limiting persistence, forcing bounded workflows and explicit termination, and avoiding per-thread stateful subagents reduces both AGII and CASX enablement.

classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: Usage context
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: No — LangGraph enables high-agency patterns, but those require explicit developer configuration of loops, persistence, subagents, and tools

langgraph.main_uncertainty: The main uncertainty is how far to credit LangGraph’s deployment and runtime ecosystem versus the core framework itself when scoring CASX; the docs clearly show strong orchestration and tool-enablement, but realized action power still depends heavily on external model and tool configuration and application-specific deployment choices.

manus.name: Manus
manus.summary: Manus is a deployed agentic AI service that accepts open-ended goals, executes multi-step tasks in a sandboxed or connected environment, and returns completed work products rather than only conversational answers. Official documentation and external testing both support that it can persist through multi-step workflows with tool use, but also that it is still unreliable, infrastructure-constrained, and often requires human clarification or correction.

primary_interpretation.driver: Realized multi-step autonomy with browser, code, scheduling, and API-mediated execution
primary_interpretation.constraint: User-initiated operation, frequent need for clarification or approval, and observed reliability limits

agii.evidence: Manus is documented as an autonomous AI agent with its own sandboxed computer, internet access, persistent file system, software installation capability, and support for long-running asynchronous tasks, state tracking, projects with shared instructions, and scheduled recurring tasks. Public descriptions indicate that tasks can continue until completion or pause when user input is needed.
agii.interpretation: This is meaningful realized persistence rather than a thin chat wrapper. Manus can maintain state over extended workflows, continue work without turn-by-turn prompting, and re-engage on recurring schedules. However, its agency pressure is still bounded because it is typically launched by a user request, often pauses for clarification on ambiguous actions, and remains imperfect in practice.
agii.implication: AGII is high for a commercial agent product, but not extreme. The main risk comes from sustained task execution and recurrence once delegated, not from unconstrained self-maintaining behavior across arbitrary goals.

casx.evidence: Manus can operate a cloud browser, click and fill forms, extract data, manage agent tasks programmatically, connect to data sources and custom MCP connections, and execute recurring scheduled tasks. It can interact with external digital environments through browser activity, authenticated sessions, integrations, files, and workflow automation.
casx.interpretation: Manus has substantial power in action because it is not limited to text generation. It can affect external digital environments through browsing, authenticated sessions, data integrations, file generation, and workflow automation. This gives it materially greater action capacity than a standalone model, though much of that power remains scoped to user-delegated tasks, specific connectors, sandboxed environments, or authenticated contexts the user exposes.
casx.implication: CASX is the more concerning axis. In practical deployments, Manus can produce real external effects in software systems, browsers, and business workflows, especially when paired with credentials, APIs, or enterprise integrations.

trajectory.evidence: Since launch, Manus has expanded from preview into paid consumer and team offerings, mobile access, API v2, browser operator, scheduled tasks, wider integrations, and enterprise-oriented features. At the same time, early third-party reporting noted server strain, invitation-only access, and gaps between marketing and observed performance.
trajectory.interpretation: The direction of change is clearly upward, but the evidence supports Large rather than Very Large. Manus is moving fast in capability surface and deployment channels, yet the current record still shows operational fragility and product immaturity.
trajectory.implication: Risk is likely to rise meaningfully as integrations, reliability, concurrency, and enterprise embedding improve. The biggest shift would come not from better reasoning alone, but from smoother execution, broader authenticated access, and easier automation at scale.

change_levers.increase_risk: Greater reliability, more unsupervised execution, broader authenticated browser and action access, richer enterprise connectors, higher task concurrency, and more default recurrence or persistence.
change_levers.decrease_risk: Stronger approval gates for consequential actions, narrower tool permissions, reduced credential scope, stricter task and runtime limits, better audit logs, and more frequent human checkpoints.

classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: Usage context, especially when connected to browsers, credentials, APIs, internal tools, or recurring workflows
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: Conditional — risk is not inherent in every interaction, but rises substantially when Manus is granted action channels, authenticated sessions, or scheduled and programmable autonomy

sources.title: Browser Operator / Cloud Browser / Scheduled Tasks / Integrations

manus.main_uncertainty: The largest uncertainty is the gap between Manus’s documented capability surface and its consistently realized behavior in unconstrained real-world use; public technical detail about internal architecture, guardrails, failure rates, and operator oversight remains limited.

openai-responses-api.name: OpenAI Responses API
openai-responses-api.summary: The OpenAI Responses API is best classified as a framework-like API surface for building agentic applications, not as a standalone agent, because it provides the execution structure, tool interfaces, state mechanisms, and long-running modes that developers can use to build agents, while the actual autonomy level depends heavily on the surrounding application design and permissions. It directly enables multi-step tool use, stateful context, background execution, and connections to external services, but it does not by itself instantiate persistent independent behavior without developer configuration and deployment choices.

primary_interpretation.driver: Native support for multi-step tool-calling loops, persistent conversation/state mechanisms, and optional long-running/background execution
primary_interpretation.constraint: Realized autonomy and impact depend on developer-supplied tools, approval settings, runtime wiring, model choice, and deployment controls rather than on the API alone

agii.evidence: OpenAI documents the Responses API as allowing multiple tool calls within one request; it supports store:true, previous_response_id, durable conversation objects via the Conversations API, and background mode for long-running tasks that continue while developers poll status. The local shell guide also states that the tool can support a continuous build-test-run loop without extra user intervention once configured.
agii.interpretation: The API materially enables persistent agency pressure: it supports chained actions, maintained state, continuation across turns, and longer-running execution. But this persistence is infrastructural rather than realized by default; the API does not itself decide goals, schedule recurring work, or maintain open-ended agency unless the developer builds those behaviors on top.
agii.implication: AGII is above ordinary stateless text APIs because the Responses API lowers the engineering barrier to multi-step and semi-persistent agent workflows, but it remains below realized agent systems because persistence is enabled, not independently enacted, under typical use.

casx.evidence: Official tools documentation says the Responses API can use built-in tools, function calling, tool search, remote MCP servers, file search, web search, computer use, code interpreter, shell, and connectors to external services. MCP/connectors can connect to and control third-party services; file search is hosted and automatically executed when selected; shell and local shell can run commands in hosted containers or user-provided environments; and computer-use guidance explicitly discusses risks from on-screen third-party content and phishing/prompt-injection scenarios.
casx.interpretation: The API enables substantial real-world power in action because it can mediate access to files, web information, code execution, terminal commands, external SaaS systems, and tool discovery. However, that power is gated: some actions require explicit developer approval, some tools are model-limited, local execution remains under developer control, and OpenAI’s own safety guidance highlights meaningful misuse and prompt-injection risks rather than presenting these capabilities as inherently safe or fully autonomous.
casx.implication: CASX is moderately high for a framework because the action pathways are real and broad, but it should stay below high-end realized agent scores since the API surface does not itself guarantee broad autonomous execution; power emerges when developers attach credentials, runtimes, and permissive policies.

trajectory.evidence: OpenAI describes Responses as the recommended API for new projects and as the successor primitive to Chat Completions for agent-like applications. The documentation shows continuing expansion in capability surface, including tool search, MCP/connectors, background mode, state management via Conversations, and specialized tools such as shell and computer use. At the same time, the docs preserve strong caveats around safety, approvals, sandboxing, retention tradeoffs, and model/tool compatibility.
trajectory.interpretation: The direction of change is clearly upward in agent-enablement: OpenAI is consolidating more agent-building functionality into the Responses stack and making it easier to build longer-running, tool-using workflows. Still, the observed evidence supports Large rather than Very Large because the API remains a developer-mediated substrate, and realized risk growth depends on what downstream builders deploy.
trajectory.implication: Expect the Responses API to raise the ceiling and accessibility of agentic systems over time, especially where developers combine it with external tools and permissive runtimes, but present evidence does not justify treating the API itself as a near-boundary realized agent.

change_levers.increase_risk: More default background execution, easier autonomous recurrence, broader built-in tool coverage, looser approval gates, richer connectors/MCP access, and stronger default state persistence would increase AGII and CASX.
change_levers.decrease_risk: Mandatory human approval for sensitive tools, tighter sandboxing, narrower tool permissions, disabling storage/state chaining, restricting shell/computer use, and limiting connector credential scope would reduce AGII and CASX.

classification_notes.where_risk_triggered: usage context in which developers expose tools, credentials, runtimes, background mode, and persistent state to model-driven workflows
classification_notes.inevitable_under_normal_use: No — the API can be used as a simple response endpoint, and the higher-risk agentic properties emerge conditionally when developers enable tools, persistence, long-running execution, or external system access

sources.title: OpenAI Migrate to the Responses API

openai-responses-api.main_uncertainty: The main uncertainty is not whether the Responses API enables agentic behavior, which is well documented, but how much realized persistence and action power typical production deployments actually instantiate, since that varies widely with model choice, tool permissions, approval policies, local versus hosted execution, and whether developers use the API as a simple inference endpoint or as the core of a long-running agent workflow.
